Although details change in various records, her parents are described as a deity (her father), and a daughter of an influential person in the [[Yamato Province]] (her mother). She is said to have married [[Emperor Jimmu]] and given birth to the second Emperor, [[Emperor Suizei|Suizei]].<ref name="illustrated-chronicle-jinmu">''Illustrated Chronicle of the Emperors of Japan'', p.37-41, "Emperor Jimmu".</ref><ref name="japanese-god-name-dictionary-2" /><!-- 伝承ごとに細部の差異はあるものの、母親はヤマト地方の有力者の娘で、父親は神であったと描かれている。神武天皇に嫁いで皇后となり、2代天皇の綏靖天皇を産んだとされている[13][2]。-->

== Depiction by ''Kojiki'' and ''Nihon Shoki'' ==

=== Birth ===<!-- taken from [[Ōmononushi]] -->

According to the ''[[Kojiki]]'', when Kamu-yamato-Iwarebiko ([[Emperor Jimmu]]) was searching for a wife, he was told about a woman named {{nihongo|[[Tamayori-hime (mother-in-law of Jimmu)|Seya-datara-hime]]|勢夜陀多良比売}} who bore a daughter after she was impregnated by [[Ōmononushi|Ōmono-nushi]] (the 'Great Deity of Miwa'). Ōmono-nushi had taken the form of a red arrow and struck Seya-datara-hime's genitals while she was [[Defecation|defecating]] in a ditch.

The future emperor wooed this daughter, named {{nihongo|Hoto-tatara-Isusuki-hime|富登多多良伊須須岐比売}} (also known as {{nihongo|Hime-tatara-isuke-yori hime|比売多多良伊須気余理比売}}, an altered form of the name which omits the word {{nihongo|hoto|ホト|"female genitals"}}), and took her as his wife.<ref name="Kojiki">{{cite book |last1=Philippi |first1=Donald L. |title=Kojiki |date=2015 |publisher=Princeton University Press |pages=115–117}}</ref><ref name="Ponsonby-Fane2014">{{cite book |author=R. A. B. Ponsonby-Fane |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UVO4AwAAQBAJ&pg=PT412 |title=Studies In Shinto & Shrines |date=3 June 2014 |publisher=Taylor & Francis |isbn=978-1-136-89301-8 |page=412}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Kadoya |first1=Atsushi |title=Ōmononushi |url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=126 |accessdate=22 September 2015 |website=Encyclopedia of Shinto |publisher=Kokugakuin University}}</ref><ref name="encyclopedia-of-shinto-2015a" />

Like the ''Kojiki'', the main narrative of the first volume of the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'' first describes Hime-tatara-isuzu-hime as the offspring of the god of Ōmono-nushi. However, the ''Nihon Shoki'' also contains an alternative story which portrays her as the child of the god {{nihongo|[[Kotoshironushi|Kotoshiro-nushi]]|事代主神}} and the goddess {{nihongo|[[Mizokuhihime|Mizoku-hime]]|溝樴姫}} - also known as {{nihongo|Tamakushi-hime|玉櫛姫}} - conceived after Kotoshiro-nushi transformed himself into a gigantic ''[[Wani (dragon)|wani]]'' and had sex with her.<ref name="shinto-dic-861" /><ref>{{cite wikisource|year=1896|plaintitle=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697|wslink=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697|wspage=61–62|chapter=Book I|publisher=Kegan Paul, Trench, Trübner & Co.|author-first=William George|author-last=Aston}}</ref> Likewise, the main narrative in the third and fourth volumes of ''Nihon Shoki'' refers to her as the daughter of Kotoshiro-nushi rather than Ōmono-nushi.<ref>{{cite wikisource|year=1896|plaintitle=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697|wslink=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697|wspage=132|chapter=Book III|publisher=Kegan Paul, Trench, Trübner & Co.|author-first=William George|author-last=Aston}}</ref><ref>{{cite wikisource|year=1896|plaintitle=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697|wslink=Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697|wspage=138|chapter=Book IV|publisher=Kegan Paul, Trench, Trübner & Co.|author-first=William George|author-last=Aston}}</ref>

Her house was located on the Sai River and near Sai-jinja Shrine, near [[Mount Miwa]].<ref name="An Encounter on the Sai River" />

=== Marriage with Emperor Jimmu ===
According to the ''Nihon Shoki'' and other sources, Iwarehiko (later Emperor Jimmu) left the ''Land of Himuka'' and made an expedition to the east, and after many battles, established his government in the [[Yamato Province|Yamato region]]. Iwarehiko built the Palace of Kashiwara in modern-day [[Kashihara, Nara|Kashihara]] at the foot of [[Mount Unebi]] and ascended to the throne as the first Emperor.<ref name="Nipponica" />

Prior to his accession to the throne, Iwarehiko needed to have a [[Queen consort|consort]] worthy of being the first Empress. Ōume-no-mikoto, a vassal of Iwarehiko, suggested Hime-tatara-isuzu-hime as a candidate for his wife.<ref name="yomitoki-jiten" /><ref name="kojiki-and-japanese-deity"/> According to the ''Kojiki'', Ōkume-no-mikoto explains the story of Hime-tatara-isuzu-hime's birth to Iwarehiko and tells him that she deserved to be his rightful wife.<ref name="ヒメたち98" /><ref name="kojiki-and-japanese-deity"/> In the ''Kojiki'', there is another story in which Iwarehiko and Ōkume-no-mikoto witnessed seven women on the shore of the Sai River and selected a wife from among them.<ref name="An Encounter on the Sai River">{{Cite web |title=An Encounter on the Sai River <!--note I am citing the English section below, not the Japanese section--> |url=https://www3.pref.nara.jp/miryoku/narakikimanyo/manabu/story/story07/ |access-date=2023-03-04 |website=www3.pref.nara.jp}}</ref>

Hime-tatara-isuzu-hime had a notable poetic exchange with them, and then Jimmu stayed the night at her house.<ref name="An Encounter on the Sai River" />

According to the ''Nihon Shoki'', their marriage took place on September 24 of the year before his accession.{{efn|In ''Nihon Shoki'', he began his search for a consort on August 16th by the [[lunar calendar]], the year before his accession to the throne,<ref name="yomitoki-jiten" /><ref name="歴代皇后-神武">"Overview of Empress Characters", p26-27 "The First Emperor Jimmu, Empress Himetatara-isuzu"</ref> and he chose Hime-tatara-isuzu-hime as her consort and married her on September 24<!-- by the lunar calendar ("September New Moon")-->.<ref name="新撰大人名辞典">Japanese Name Dictionary, p.262 "Hime-tatara-isuzu-hime no Mikoto</ref><ref name="womens-name-876">''Japanese Women's Name Dictionary, Popular Edition'' p.876 "Hime-tatara-isuzu-hime-[m]"</ref>}} Hime-tatara-isuzu-hime became Empress when Emperor Jimmu ascended the throne in the following year, 660 BC.{{efn|In Nihon Shoki, the year of Emperor Jimmu's accession to the throne is taken as the year of the "{{lang|ja|辛酉, Shin-Yū, Kanoto-tori}}" (the year in [[Sexagenary cycle]]. See "[[:ja:辛酉|ja Article]]"). According to the calculation method established in the Meiji era (1868-1912), taking into account the [[:ja:讖緯|Shin'i theory]] (Chinese prophecy theory) and the "Shin-Yu Revolution theory", this year is [[660 BC]]. In the past, this was considered a historical fact, but it is not usually considered a fact at present.<ref name="illustrated-chronicle-jinmu" /> For more information, see [[Japanese imperial year]].}}

=== After the death of Emperor Jimmu ===
According to the ''Nihon Shoki'', Emperor Jimmu died at the age of 127. Although there are differences in details, the ''Nihon Shoki'' and ''Kojiki'' describe a succession struggle that occurred among his children after his death.

Before he left for the eastern expedition from the "Land of Himuka", Iwarehiko had married Airatsu-hime ({{lang|ja|吾平津媛}}) and they had child.<ref name="yomitoki-jiten" />{{efn|The "Kojiki" records the names of two of his children. [[Tagishimimi|Tagishi-mimi]] (<ref name="日本神名辞典-多芸">Nihon Shinmei Jiten (Dictionary of the Japanese Gods), p235 "Tagishi-mimi".</ref>) and [[Kisumimi|Kisu-mimi]] (<ref name="日本神名辞典-岐須">Nihon Shinmei Jiten (Dictionary of the Divine Names of Japan), p151 "Kisumimi-no-mikoto".</ref>).<ref name="読み解き事典-阿比良">Nihon no Kami Yomitoki Jiten (A Dictionary of Japanese Gods and Goddesses), p.40-41 "Airatsu-hime"</ref><ref name="歴代天皇Shoki-綏靖">Illustrated Chronicle of the Emperors of Japan, p.42-43, "Emperor Suizei</ref> On the other hand, the ''Nihon Shoki'' only mentions the name of [[Tagishimimi|Tagishi-mimi no mikoto]] and does not mention the name of the person corresponding to Kisu-mimi no mikoto.<ref name="読み解き事典-阿比良"/>}} However, these children were reduced to the status of [[Bastard child|bastards]] when Iwarehiko made Hime-tatara-isuzu-hime the rightful Empress. When Emperor Jimmu died, his bastard son, Tagishi-mimi, wanted to succeed to the throne himself.{{efn|According to Nihon Shoki and other sources, Tagishi-mimi served under Emperor Jimmu for a long time. but he was described as having a difficult personality and a tendency to "disobey humanity".<ref name="歴代天皇Shoki-綏靖"/> These descriptions are not necessarily considered to be the true historical facts. When [[Emperor Suizei]] succeeded his father [[Emperor Jimmu]], the [[ultimogeniture]] took place, which is thought to have been common in ancient Japan. However, later on [[primogeniture]] became common, and some people required the proper reasons which could explain the exclusion of Tagishi-mimi from the right of succeeding the throne, this story, in which Tagishi-mimi, an eldest son who is a legitimate inheritant in the primogeniture system, was a bad person and planned the rebellion, could satisfy them.<ref name="歴代天皇Shoki-綏靖"/>}}

In the ''Kojiki'', Tagishi-mimi took the widowed Empress Hime-tatara-isuzu-hime as his wife and tried to assassinate the legitimate children of Emperor Jimmu and Empress Hime-tatara-isuzu-hime. Aware of his plans, Hime-tatara-isuzu-hime wrote two poems to her children to warn them of the danger.<ref name="ヒメたち98">Hime in Mythology: The Other Kojiki, p98-101 "The First Empress Who Saved Her Son with a Song".</ref>{{Refn|In the ''Kojiki'', "天皇崩後、其庶兄當藝志美美命、娶其嫡后伊須気持余理比売之時、將殺其三弟而謀之間、其御祖伊須気持余理比売之患苦而、以歌令知其御子等" [roughly] After the demise of the Emperor, when the bastard son, Tagishi-mimi, married Isuke-yori-hime, the Empress Dowager, and he wanted to assassinate his three younger brothers, the mother Isuke-yori-hime was distressed and notified this conspiration to her sons by the songs. (''Kojiki'', 1963, Iwanami bunko, p.101).|group="Kojiki"}}

Learning of the plot from their mother's poems, the legitimate sons attacked Tagishi-mimi first and defeated him. Kan-nunakawa-mimi no mikoto ({{lang|ja|神渟名川耳命, or 神沼河耳命}}), who played the most active role in the attack, succeeded his father and ascended to the throne as the second emperor, [[Emperor Suizei]]. According to the ''Nihon Shoki'', Hime-tatara-isuzu-hime took the title of "[[Empress Dowager]]".

[[Emperor Suizei]] took Princess [[Isuzuyori-hime]] ({{lang|ja|五十鈴依媛命}}) as his [[Queen consort|consort]]. Isuzu-yori-hime was Hime-tatara-isuzu hime's younger sister and [[Emperor Suizei]]'s aunt. Other versions of this story claim that Kawamata-hime (Kawamata-bime, {{lang|ja|河俣毘売}}) or Ito-ori-hime ({{lang|ja|糸織媛}}) became [[Emperor Suizei]]'s consort.

=== Children ===
Based on the ''Nihon Shoki'' and the ''Kojiki'', Hime-tatara-isuzu-hime and Emperor Jimmu had three children: [[Hikoyai|Hiko-yai]] ({{lang|ja|日子八井命}}), [[Kamuyaimimi|Kan-yai-mimi]] ({{lang|ja|神八井耳命}}), and [[Emperor Suizei]].<ref name="womens-name-876" /> Hiko-yai is only mentioned in the ''Kojiki'', whereas the other two children are mentioned in both texts. Kan-yai-mimi became the founder of the [[Ō clan]] ({{lang|ja|多氏}}).

{{A genealogical tree based on the Kojiki}}

=== Siblings ===
Himetataraisuzu-hime's mother gave birth to two other children:
* [[Kamo no Okimi|Ama-no-higata-Kushi-no-higata no mikoto]] ({{lang|ja|天日方奇日方}}), alias [[Kamo no Okimi|Kamo-no-kimi]] - Hime-tatara-isuzu-hime's elder brother. In the ''[[Kujiki]]'', he served [[Emperor Jimmu]] and became the ''osu-kuni-no-matsurigoto-mōsu-machigimi'' ({{lang|ja|申食国政大夫}}) [corresponding to Prime Minister]<!--おすくにのまつりごともうすまちぎみ-->.<ref name="himetachi-94-97" />
* [[Isuzuyori-hime|Isuzu-yori-hime]] ({{lang|ja|五十鈴依媛命}}) - Hime-tatara-isuzu-hime's sister. She became the Empress of the second emperor, [[Emperor Suizei]].<ref name="himetachi-94-97" /><ref>『図説 歴代天皇紀』p42-43「綏靖天皇」</ref>

== Various theories about her lineage ==
<!-- {{Incomprehensible|date=March 2023|sect=section}} -->
In the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'' and the ''[[Kojiki]]'', although the details of the stories differ, Hime-tatara-isuzu-hime's mother is depicted as the daughter of the influential person (a deity) of the local region (Northern [[Osaka prefecture|Osaka]]) and her father is the deity.<ref name="himetachi-94-97">''Princesses in Myths - Another Kojiki'',<!--『神話の中のヒメたち もうひとつの古事記』--> p.94-97, "The first empress is ''the child of god''".<!--「初代皇后は「神の御子」」--></ref> There is a theory which interprets that by marrying "''the child of god''" (Hime-tatara-isuzu-hime) as his principal wife, Jimmu, the first Emperor, made use of her in order to legitimize his regime.<ref name="himetachi-94-97" /><!-- 『日本書紀』と『古事記』では、説話の細部が異なるものの、ヒメタタライスズヒメは「在地の有力者（神）の娘」を母とし、「神」を父として描かれている[32]。初代天皇である神武天皇が正妻を迎えるにあたり、「神の娘」を娶ることが、神武天皇の政権の正当性を裏打ちするものとして利用されたのだろうと解釈する説がある[32]。-->

The ''Shoki'' and ''Kojiki'' also depict her maternal family as being people of Mishima ({{lang|ja|三嶋, 三島}}) in Settsu (present day [[Osaka Prefecture]]), and her paternal family being people of Miwa ({{lang|ja|美和}}, {{lang|ja|三輪}}, {{lang|ja|三輪山}}) in the Yamato region. These stories suggest the cooperation of several powerful clans in Kinki region.{{efn|『日本書紀』が説くようにヒメタタライスズヒメの父が事代主神あるいは大国主とするならば、ヒメタタライスズヒメは近畿地方の豪族に加えて出雲地方にもルーツがあるということになる。<ref name="himetachi-94-97" />}} There is also a theory which interprets this marriage as showing that the influential persons of Kawachi province (that is, Yamato and Settsu provinces){{efn|Strictly saying, it was the later time when [[Provinces of Japan]] such as Yamato and Settsu were established.}} might support a foreigner, Iwarehiko (emperor Jimmu), who came from the Himuka (Hyūga province) who marries locally.<ref name="himetachi-94-97" /><ref name="kojiki-and-japanese-deity">『古事記と日本の神々がわかる本』p90-91「イスケヨリヒメの物語」</ref> In addition, another theory interprets that this gain of support through marriage shows the political methods used by Jimmu, with him not only suppressing local powers through military power, but also through conciliatory measures towards those with local influence, as he tried to consolidate his base of control. Finally, there is also an interpretation that this story works to explain how Emperor Jimmu's forces had acquired iron-manufacturing technology.<ref name="suzumoto-1979">鈴本禎一（[[日本化学会]]）,[[doi:10.20665/kagakukyouiku.27.1_24|「たたら製鉄と和鋼記念館」]] 1979年 『化学教育』1979年27巻1号 24-27, {{doi|10.20665/kagakukyouiku.27.1_24}}<!-- 2018年7月30日閲覧。--></ref>

=== Grandfather: Mizokuhi of Mishima ===
In the ''Nihon Shoki'', her mother is said to be the daughter of '''Mishima no Mizokuhi''' ({{lang|ja|三嶋溝杙}}), although there are some differences in wording.{{efn|Mizokuhi is also written as 溝樴, 溝樴耳神, and 溝杙. In the ''Kojiki'', 湟咋 is used. Also, sometimes, 溝杭 ([[Shinsen Shōjiroku]]) or 溝咋 are used.<ref name="yamazaki-2013" /><ref name="yomitoki-jiten" /><!-- [10] -->}} Since there are some historical records in which "{{lang|ja|-耳神}}" (literally: ''god of ears'') is added to his name, there is a theory that this suggests Mizukuhi is an object of worship as a divine being.<ref name="yamazaki-2013"><!-- ja-34 -->山﨑かおり、「[https://doi.org/10.20620/nihonbungaku.62.2_1 伊須気余理比売の誕生 －神武記丹塗矢伝承の背景－]」 『日本文学』 2013年 62巻 2号 p.1-11, {{doi|10.20620/nihonbungaku.62.2_1}} , 2018年7月30日閲覧。</ref> This god (Mizukuhi) also has the names such as Suetsu-mimi-no-mikoto ({{lang|ja|陶津耳命}}), [[Kamotaketsunumi no Mikoto|Kamo-taketsunumi-no-mikoto]] ({{lang|ja|賀茂建角身命}}) and [[Yatagarasu]] ({{lang|ja|八咫烏}}), and is considered as the ancestor god of the [[Kamo clan]] and Katsuragi-no-kuni-no-miyatsuko ({{lang|ja|葛城国造}}, [[:ja:葛城国造|ja]]) in the genealogy of the Kamo clan.<ref name="houga-2015">Hōga Toshio ([[:ja:宝賀寿男]]「三輪氏の起源と動向」『古代氏族の研究⑦ 三輪氏 大物主神の祭祀者』青垣出版、2015年。></ref><!--  「-耳神」を付す史料があることから、神性をもつ存在として信仰の対象であったことも示唆されると見る説がある[34]。この神は陶津耳命や加茂建角身命、八咫烏の名を持っており、賀茂氏の系図では賀茂氏や葛城国造の祖神とされている[35]。-->

The place name "Mishima" is thought to be [[Mishima District, Osaka|Mishima county]] in [[Settsu Province]] (Northern [[Osaka Prefecture]]). The [[Engishiki]] (927) lists Mishima Kamo-jinja (located at Mishima-e, [[Takatsuki|Takatsuki City]]) and Mizokui-jinja ([[Ibaraki, Osaka|Ibaraki City]]), suggesting that "Mizokuhi of Mishima" was worshipped in this area.<ref name="yomitoki-jiten" /><ref name="yamazaki-2013" />{{efn|{{ill|Mizokui Shrine|ja|溝咋神社}} refers to Mishima no Mizokuhi as the founder of the shrine<ref name="yomitoki-jiten" /> and says that the Mishima clan would have been a powerful clan in the ancient Kawachi region.<ref name="himetachi-94-97" />}}

In the Edo period, [[Motoori Norinaga]], a scholar of [[Kokugaku]], interpreted this "''mizo'' (groove)" to refer to a [[toilet (room)|toilet]] built over a stream of water, and this has become a prevailing view.<ref name="yamazaki-2013" /> Eiichi Mitani and others have adopted this theory. There is also a theory that the toilet is strongly related to birth rituals. Kazuo Higo insists a different theory, saying that "''mizo''" means a ditch in a paddy field. Masayuki Tsugita develops this theory, claiming that Mishima-gun (Mishima county) was an ideal place for rice cultivation and that "Mishima no Mizukuhi" was a farming god.<ref name="yamazaki-2013" />

=== Mothers: Tamakushi-hime and Seya-datara-hime ===
Her mother's name is Tamakushi-hime in the ''Nihon Shoki''<ref name="yomitoki-jiten" /> and Seya-datara-hime in the ''Kojiki''.<!-- 6, 23 --> Both are said to have been known as beautiful women.<ref name="shinto-dic-861" /><ref name="womens-name-876" />{{Refn|In the ''Nihon Shoki'', "是国色之秀者".|group="Shoki"}}{{Refn|In the ''Kojiki'', "其容姿麗美".|group="Kojiki"}}

[[Motoori Norinaga]] identifies Seya ({{lang|ja|勢夜}}) as Seno village of Heguri-gun in [[Yamato Province]] ([[Sangō, Nara|Sangō Town]] of [[Ikoma District, Nara|Ikoma County]] in [[Nara Prefecture]]).<ref name="shinto-dic-861">''Shinto Daijiten (abredged version)'', p.861, "Seya-datara-hime"</ref><!-- [[大和国]][[平群郡]]勢野村（[[奈良県]][[生駒郡]][[三郷町]]）に比定している -->

=== Anecdotes of her birth in ''Kojiki'' ===
In the ''[[Kojiki]]'', she is said to be the daughter of [[Ōmononushi|Ōmono-nushi]].{{efn|Ōmono-nushi (大物主神) was originally the [[clan deity]] of the [[Mount Miwa]].<ref name="ニッポニカ-大物主">The [[Encyclopedia Nipponica]], [[Shogakukan]], 1984-1994, "Ōmono-nushi" [https://kotobank.jp/word/大物主神-450980 kotobank version], viewed 30 July 2018</ref> On the other hand, Ōmono-nushi may be another name for [[Okuninushi|Ōkuni-nushi]] (a descendant of [[Susanoo]]), and in ''Nihon Shoki'', Ōmono-nushi is the [[Mitama]] of Ōkuni-nushi.<ref name="ニッポニカ-大物主"/> Both were originally considered to be different deities.<ref name="大辞林-大物主">[[Daijirin|Daijirin Third Edition]], [[Sanseidō]], "Omono-nushi" [https://kotobank.jp/word/大物主神-450980 Kotobank version], viewed 30 July 2018.</ref><ref name="朝日人物-大物主">Asahi Nihon Rekishi Jinbutsu Jiten (Encyclopedia of Japanese Historical Figures), [[Asahi Shimbun]], 1994, "Ōmono-nushi" [https://kotobank.jp/word/大物主神-450980 kotobank version], viewed 30 July 2018.</ref>}} His birthplace is [[Mount Miwa]] in the Yamato region.

She is said to have originally been named '''Hoto-tatara-isusuki-hime'''. It is also said that she was a beautiful woman like her mother.

However, she disliked the word "''hoto''" (female genitalia) and changed her name to '''Hime-tatara-isuzu-hime'''. The dropping of the "hoto" may be related to the word being linked to genitals.<ref name="digital-museum-2023a" />

== Relation to ''tatara'' iron manufacturing==
There is a theory that the "''tatara''" ({{lang|ja|蹈鞴}}) part of the name Hime-tatara-isuzu-hime is interpreted in connection with [[Tatara (furnace)|''tatara'' iron manufacturing]], indicating iron manufacturing in ancient Japan.<ref name="鈴本1979"/><ref name="小路田2005"/><ref name="kojiki-and-japanese-deity"/>{{efn|The character "鞴" used in Nihon Shoki refers to the [[bellows]] used in iron making.<ref name="小路田2005">{{ill|Yasunao Kojita|ja|小路田泰直}} ([[Nara Women's University]], History),[http://nwudir.lib.nara-wu.ac.jp/dspace/bitstream/10935/433/1/20080522_2.pdf "The 'Kojiki' and 'Nihonshoki'. Narrating the History of the Formation of the Japanese State : From the Perspective of Fire and Iron"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180730170613/http://nwudir.lib.nara-wu.ac.jp/dspace/bitstream/10935/433/1/20080522_2.pdf |date=2018-07-30 }}, 2005 (Methods in Japanese History, No. 2 pp. 145-168), viewed 30 July 2018.</ref>}}{{efn|In modern Japan (before the gathering of the [[World War II]]), the origins of iron manufacturing in Japan have been traced back to the "period of gods" ({{lang|ja|神代}}, ''kamiyo'' or ''shindai''),<ref name="鈴本1979">Teiichi Suzumoto ([[Chemical Society of Japan]]),[https://doi.org/10.20665/kagakukyouiku.27.1_24 "Tatara Iron and Wako Memorial Hall"], 1979 Journal of Chemical Education, 1979, vol. 27, no. 1, 24-27, {{doi|10.20665/kagakukyouiku.27.1_24}}, viewed 30 July 2018.</ref> with episodes in the ''Nihon Shoki'' and the ''Kojiki'' stating that when [[Amaterasu]] hid in [[Amano-Iwato]], iron from "Ama-no-kaguyama ({{lang|ja|天香山}}, in ''Nihon Shoki'')" or "Ame-no-kanayama ({{lang|ja|天金山}}, in ''Kojiki'')" was used for metalworking. (Nihon Shoki)" or "Amakinzan (Kojiki)".<ref name="鈴本1979"/><ref name="進藤1975">Yoshihiko Shindo (Institute for Asian Studies, [[Asia University (Japan)|Asia University]]),[http://id.nii.ac.jp/1385/00013673/ "A Study on the Origin of Ironware Culture in Ancient Japan"], 1975 Journal of the College of Liberal Arts, Asia University, 12, 99-118, viewed 30 July 2018.</ref> In modern times, it is generally accepted that iron making technology was introduced from mainland China along with rice cultivation,<ref name="進藤1975"/> but archaeological evidence is insufficient,<ref name="進藤1975"/> and no definitive theory has been established about its origin or age.<ref name="鈴本1979"/> In terms of literary sources, iron manufacturing is specifically detailed in the {{ill|Izumono Kuni Fudoki|ja|出雲国風土記}} of the 8th century, and it is thought that iron manufacturing was already established in this period.<ref name="鈴本1979"/>}}{{efn|Teiichi Suzumoto ([[Chemical Society of Japan]]) has argued that the huge [[Emperor Nintoku#Nintoku's tomb|Emperor Nintoku's Mausoleum]], which dates from around the early 5th century, was probably made possible to build by the establishment of iron tools, and that the [[Yamato Kingship|Yamato Imperial Court]] of the time probably had secured [[Tatara (furnace)|tatara iron]] technology.<ref name="鈴本1979"/> Fuigo has been excavated from the {{ill|Higashi Nara Ruins|ja|東奈良遺跡}} (in [[Ibaraki, Osaka|Ibaraki City]], [[Osaka Prefecture]]), and some have linked this to iron manufacturing by the Yamato Court.<ref name="吉野1975">Hiroshi Yoshino,[https://doi.org/10.20620/nihonbungaku.24.8_75 "The Story of Tara and Ota Taneko (Qicaian Zoso III)"], Japanese Literature, 1975, vol. 24, no. 8, p. 75-83, {{doi|10.20620/nihonbungaku.24.8_75}}, viewed on July 30, 2018.</ref> At this Higashinara site (discovered in 1971), [[Dōtaku]] and their casts have been excavated, and it is certain that bronze bells were made there.<ref name="ブリタニカ-東奈良遺跡">''[[Britannica International Encyclopedia|Britannica International Encyclopedia of Minor Subjects]]'', 2014, "East Nara Site" [https://kotobank.jp/word/東奈良遺跡-119134 kotobank version], viewed 30 July 2018.</ref>}}

According to {{ill|Yasunao Kojita|ja|小路田泰直}}, ''tatara'' refers to a "tatara furnace", and ''hoto'' refers to "fireplace" as well as "female genitalia".<ref name="yasunao-kojita-2005a">{{cite web |url= http://www.kunaicho.go.jp/e-about/genealogy/img/keizu-e.pdf |title= 
History of the formation of the Japanese nation as told by" Kojiki "and" Nihon Shoki ": From the perspective of fire and iron"|author= Yasunao Kojita |date=October 7, 2010 |publisher= Nara Women's University, History |page= 145-168|access-date=October 25, 2025 |url-status=dead
|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20180730170613/http://nwudir.lib.nara-wu.ac.jp/dspace/bitstream/10935/433/1/20080522_2.pdf |archive-date=July 30, 2018  }}</ref>{{efn|The word "hoto" (溶鉱炉) also refers to "blast furnace".<ref name="吉野1975"/>}} In other words, the fact that Emperor Jimmu took Hime-tatara-isuzu-hime (= Hime-tatara-isuke-yori-hime = Hoto-tatara-isusuki-hime)<!-- ヒメタタライスズヒメ（=ヒメタタライスケヨリヒメ=ホトタタライススキヒメ）--> as his wife is interpreted as an indication that the royal family controlled the iron and steel industry.<ref name="yasunao-kojita-2005a" /> Yutaka Yoshino (Japan Literature Association) states that the name "Hoto-tatara-isuzu-hime" refers to a priestess who served the god of molten ore and the blast furnace.<ref name="裕-1975a">{{Cite journal |last=裕 |first=吉野 |date=1975 |title=タタラと大田田根子の話(其蜩庵雑草 Iii) |url=https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/nihonbungaku/24/8/24_KJ00010006430/_article/-char/ja/ |journal=日本文学 |volume=24 |issue=8 |pages=75–83 |doi=10.20620/nihonbungaku.24.8_75}}</ref>

[[Motoori Norinaga]] and other early modern [[Kokugaku]] scholars did not interpret the word "''tatara''" in Hime-tatara-isuzu-hime to mean a bellows.<ref name="裕-1975a" /> In their view, the word ''tatara'' is a slang term used by blacksmiths and is dismissed from its ties to steelmaking as it is unsuitable for the name of a noble empress.<ref name="裕-1975a" /> "Some interpret "''tatara''" as a derivative of "stand", meaning "stood up (surprised by an arrow in the pubic region)" or "had an arrow put up (in the pubic region).<ref name="shinto-dic-1227" /><ref name="japanese-god-name-dictionary-2" />

== Objects of faith==
[[Emperor Meiji]] founded the [[Kashihara Shrine|Kashihara Jingu]] in 1890, where Emperor Jimmu and Hime-tathara-isuzu-hime are enshrined as the main deities.<ref name="shinto-dic-1227">Shinto Daijiten (abredged edition), p.1227, "Hime-tatara-isuzt-hime-[m]".</ref><ref name="日本神名辞典-比売">Nihon Shinmei Jiten (Dictionary of the Japanese Gods), p320 "Hiyotara Isuke Yorihime".</ref>。

Hime-tatara-isuzu-hime also came to be revered as a "{{Nihongo|2=子守明神|3=Komori Myōjin}}" because she saved children, and is enshrined as the main deity at {{Interlanguage link|Isagawa Shrine|ja|率川神社}} (Honkomori-cho, Nara City, Nara Prefecture).<ref name="神話の中のヒメたち-もうひとつの古事記-3">『神話の中のヒメたち もうひとつの古事記』p98-101「歌で御子救った初代皇后」」</ref>{{efn|The {{ill|Isagawa Shrine|ja|率川神社}} is a regent shrine of the Miwasan and [[Ōmiwa Shrine]], which is said to be the hometown of Himetataraisuhime.<ref name="ヒメたち98"/>}} In June of every year, the Nitsukawa Shrine holds the "Saegusa Festival" (commonly known as the ''Yuri'' festival, {{lang|ja|三枝祭}}, alias {{lang|ja|ゆり祭り}}), where Hime-tatara-isuzu-hime is worshipped by offering ''lilies'' grown at [[Mount Miwa]].<ref name="神話の中のヒメたち-もうひとつの古事記-3" /><!-- This "ゆり (yuri)" is not Western "lily". This is "ささゆり (sasayuri)". edit Later ++++++++ -->

At the upper reaches of the {{Nihongo|Sakai River|狭井川}}, where Himetataraisuzu-hime's parents lived, there is the {{Nihongo|Sakai Shrine|狭井神社}}. Here, the main deity is Himetataraisuzu-hime, but also [[Ōmononushi|Omononushi]] (father of Himetataraisuzu-hime according to the ''Kojiki''), Seyadatara-hime (mother of Himetataraisuzu-hime according to the ''Kojiki''), [[Kotoshironushi|Kotoshirohime]] (mother of Himetataraisuzu-hime according to the ''Kojiki'') [[Tamayori-hime (mother-in-law of Jimmu)|Tamayori-hime]], [[Kotoshironushi]] (father of Himetataraisukehime according to the ''Nihon Shoki'') are enshrined here.<ref>『日本歴史地名大系30奈良県の地名』p435-436「狭井神社」</ref>

She is also worshipped at Tsumori Jingu Shrine ([[Kumamoto Prefecture]] [[Kamimashiki District, Kumamoto|Kamimashiki District]] [[Mashiki, Kumamoto|Mashiki Town]]) and {{ill|Kosa Shrine|ja|甲佐神社}} ([[Kōsa, Kumamoto|Kosa Town]]).<ref>『日本の神仏の辞典』p1094「ひめたたらいすずひめのみこと」</ref>
